column3: Shares the interrogative opening and presents a figure who turns away, but adds little to the specific boast.
Corrects the assumption that possessed wealth is good by showing its judgment-day consequence.
Directly frames wealth and children as a test rather than proof of secure favor.
The garden owner's comparison of wealth and children closely parallels arrogant material boasting.
Uses birth and resurrection language for Jesus, not the claimant's promised wealth and offspring.
Its condemnation of human ingratitude broadly frames the disbelief named in the focus ayah.
God's granting of abundant wealth to a denier contrasts with treating wealth as a self-guaranteed entitlement.
The immediate question directly exposes the boast as dependent on unseen knowledge or a covenant with the Merciful.
Warns that wealth and children can distract from God's remembrance, countering their value as a boast.
Records a boast about expending heaps of wealth, a limited parallel to self-assured material speech.
The immediate continuation reverses the possession claim: God inherits what is claimed and the person arrives alone.
Treats worldly life and wealth as secondary to faith and reverence, broadly qualifying the focus claim.
The wealth-hoarder who counts his possessions gives a close pattern of materially grounded delusion.
Directly questions whether the deniers possess knowledge of the unseen, the issue raised by the focus claim.
States the grave condition of disbelieving wrongdoers but adds no specific wealth, children, or future-claim link.
The speaker boasts of greater wealth and a stronger following, closely matching the social claim behind the focus ayah.
Identifies Jesus amid dispute and does not clarify the denier's promised possessions.
Giving wealth for purification supplies a distant ethical contrast to boasting about receiving it.
Its rhetorical challenge to prolonged worldly enjoyment anticipates the futility of the claimed future prosperity.
The immediate denial answers the boast with recording of the speech and an extension of punishment.
Uses wealth for striving in God's cause, offering only a general contrast to material self-assertion.
Explicit denial of God's signs matches the focus ayah's defining charge.
The nearby resurrection argument challenges a human being's confidence about a future possession after death.
Describes persistent unbelief generally, without adding to the particular claim in the focus ayah.
Belief in God's signs provides a general opposite to the disbelief stated in the focus ayah.
Affirms that every hidden matter is recorded, countering a claim premised on access to the unseen.
The claim that the Merciful has a child is a different issue despite the shared offspring term.
Links disbelief in God's signs to an adverse final outcome, extending the focus ayah's warning.
Calls Jesus a sign for people, but does not develop rejection of signs or the possession claim.
Forbids exalting oneself against God, a broad rebuke relevant to the claimant's presumption.
Shows a denier whose God-given kingship becomes grounds for arrogant argument before being confounded.
Assigns expansion and restriction of provision to God, directly contesting self-assured claims of future wealth.
Pictures deniers facing a hard day, a general judgment consequence for the disbelief in the focus.
Ad's boast of superior strength and denial of signs parallels self-exalting disbelief before divine power.
Continues the theological dispute about attributing a child to the Merciful, not the focus claim.
Directly denies that wealth and children can avail their possessors against God.
Contrasts grateful recognition that a gift is from God with the focus figure's presumptive future claim.
Jesus's blessings and worship commands do not clarify the denier's boast.
Division after clear evidence only broadly resembles refusal of revealed signs.
The interrogative exposure of one ruled by desire offers a close general portrait of willful misguidance.
Joseph's concealment and the private revelation are unrelated to the focus claim.
The statement about despair and disbelief does not add a material or unseen-claim relation.
Contrasts those who believe in God's signs with the focus figure's disbelief.
Rejects divine offspring and does not address the human claim to offspring and wealth.
States that God's favor is given as He wills, broadly qualifying the asserted future receipt.
A real divine covenant, with stated conditions and consequences, contrasts with the claimant's unproved covenant claim.
The same-surah setting shows deniers answering clear signs by boasting of superior station and assembly.
Spending wealth for God's cause is only a broad contrast to relying on wealth as status.
Addresses a distinct doctrinal denial about the Messiah rather than the focus figure's boast.
Jesus's dutifulness to his mother has no material relation to the focus ayah.
The conditional rejection of divine offspring is a different use of the offspring term.
Deniers are confronted for rejecting their Lord's signs after warning, extending the focus's consequence.
The later reversal of false worshipers and their objects belongs to the same denunciation of the deniers.
Directly states that wealth will not avail a person at ruin.
Solomon's grateful prayer for righteous action does not develop the focus claim.
God as the best inheritor gives a distant contrast to confidence in retaining offspring.
Notes disbelief in the revelation and its eventual consequence, but without the focus's distinctive boast.
The proposed adoption of Joseph is unrelated to the claimant's promised children.
Rejects divine offspring and does not explain the focus figure's claim.
Depicts deniers rushing toward the Prophet, with no added connection to wealth or unseen knowledge.
The signs and station of Abraham do not clarify the response to the focus ayah.
The nearby sorting of those most deserving of Hell broadly supplies the passage's judgment horizon.
Models reliance on God to give from His bounty, contrasting with a denier's self-guaranteed future receipt.
The general parent-and-child expression adds no relevant claim or judgment relation.
Directly voices the boast of greater wealth and children and the presumption of immunity from punishment.
Directly denies that a person's wealth and earnings can avail him.
The statement about God neither begetting nor being begotten is unrelated to the human boast.
God's creation from nothing offers only a distant background to the nearby resurrection argument.
Describes a particular corrupt worship practice, not the focus claim.
Shares the interrogative address and directly names denial and turning away.
Pharaoh's arrogant attempt to reach the heavens and denial of Moses is only a broad parallel of presumptuous disbelief.
Directly negates the value of wealth and children on the day of judgment.
Shows the response to recited signs as dismissing them as ancient tales, closely paralleling rejection of signs.
The immediate sequel identifies demonic incitement of the deniers, extending the focus passage's account of them.
States that disbelief and obstruction nullify deeds, a general consequence beyond the focus's particular speech.
Repeats the same response to recited signs as 68:15 but adds no new value after that earlier card.
Destroyed communities made insolent by ease provide a broader warning against prosperity-based complacency.
A promise of great reward from God only distantly contrasts with the denier's asserted future grant.
An outrageous statement about God is too general to clarify the focus claim.
Ishmael's faithful household leadership does not develop the material boast or its rebuttal.
The command to cast every stubborn denier into Hell supplies a general final consequence.
The reference to Moses as a child is narrative context unrelated to promised offspring.
The abundance of Paradise fruit does not clarify the focus figure's claim.
Disbelief makes spending unacceptable, giving a meaningful contrast to treating wealth as proof of favor.
A people's accusation against Noah does not bear on the claim to wealth and children.
God's making the oppressed inheritors provides only a general counterpoint to worldly status claims.
Rejects divine offspring, a distinct theological issue from the human's assertion.
Shares the interrogative opening but its prohibition scene does not materially explain the focus ayah.
God's granting of power in the land broadly contrasts with the denier's claimed control of his future.
The angels' assurance of truth in Lot's narrative does not relate to the focus claim.
False worldly attachments become mutual rejection at judgment, fitting the passage's reversal of worldly securities.
The summons of skilled magicians is unrelated to the focus ayah.
God's guardianship of the righteous does not clarify the denier's boast.
The difficulty of the day for deniers provides a general consequence for the focus's disbelief.
God's true binding promise to believers contrasts with the denier's unsupported claim of a covenant.
Directly denies that kinship and children will benefit anyone on the Day of Resurrection.
Inheritance rules for children do not bear on the claimant's promised wealth and offspring.
God's gift of wisdom and the contrast between gratitude and disbelief offer only a broad ethical relation.
The fire sent against humans and jinn is too general to add to the focus ayah.
Deniers demand the threatened punishment, broadly paralleling defiant disbelief in divine warning.
Directly states that the wealth and children of disbelievers will not avail them before God.
Names the love of sons and accumulated wealth as worldly attraction rather than final good.
Again directly denies that disbelievers' wealth and children can avail them before God.
The people of the heights tell arrogant people that their amassed wealth did not avail them.
Warns against admiring disbelievers' wealth and children, which become a means of punishment.
Recalls earlier people stronger and richer in wealth and children who merely enjoyed their worldly share.
Repeats the warning that wealth and children of disbelievers are not signs of favor but a punishment.
Moses describes Pharaoh's wealth and splendor as a means by which people are led astray.
Those seeking only worldly life and its adornment receive their works there but lose the hereafter.
Satan's promised participation in wealth and children exposes both as possible instruments of deception.
The garden owner claims his wealth will never perish, closely matching unwarranted future security.
He doubts the Hour yet expects a better return to his Lord, a very close parallel to the focus claim.
The destruction of the garden visibly overturns the owner's confidence in his possessions.
Wealth and children are called the adornment of worldly life, while enduring righteous deeds are better with God.
The deniers take other gods to obtain honor, extending the passage's critique of imagined worldly security.
Specifies who can possess a covenant with the Merciful, directly clarifying the question posed in 19:78.
Worldly splendor is a test, not an object to covet, directly qualifying material display as favor.
Long enjoyment of disbelievers and their forefathers illustrates the temporary extension of worldly ease.
Questions whether the wealth and sons granted to deniers mean that God is hastening good to them.
Completes the rebuke of mistaking extended wealth and sons for divine favor.
Qarun's immense wealth leads him to transgress, providing a narrative warning against wealth-based arrogance.
Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge, paralleling presumptuous claims about material possession.
Qarun's being swallowed with his dwelling decisively overturns confidence in amassed wealth.
Directly denies that a child can avail a parent, or a parent a child, on the Day of Judgment.
States that wealth and children do not bring people near to God, except through faith and righteous action.
A person claims a bestowed favor came through personal knowledge, a close form of presumptive entitlement.
A person doubts the Hour yet claims that, if returned to God, he will have the best reward.
Describes worldly material provision as a possible allotment even for those who disbelieve in the Merciful.
Continues the picture of lavish worldly possessions given without implying true favor.
Explicitly calls such wealth merely enjoyment of worldly life, while the hereafter belongs to the reverent.
Places wealth and children among the attractions and rivalry of worldly life that ultimately fade.
Directly calls wealth and children a test and places the great reward with God instead.
The condemned person confesses that his wealth did not avail him.
At judgment, the guilty person would seek ransom even through his own children, overturning reliance on them.
God's promised increase of wealth and sons follows repentance, contrasting true divine granting with the denier's claim.
The denier's sons kept before him form part of the same wealth-and-status pattern as the focus ayah.
God's expansive ease granted to the denier contrasts with treating such provision as self-secured.
The denier's craving for further increase closely parallels the focus figure's assertion of future abundance.
His stubbornness toward God's signs directly joins material privilege to the disbelief named in the focus.
A human reads abundant provision as proof that his Lord has honored him, a direct critique of material inference.
The same human reads restricted provision as humiliation, completing the correction of wealth-based status judgment.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts people until death, broadly exposing the danger of material competition.
